source.title: Scaling Laws for BERT in Low-Resource Settings
source.authors: Gorka Urbizu; Iñaki San Vicente; X. Saralegi; Rodrigo Agerri; Aitor Soroa Etxabe

record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling results in low-resource BERT settings and reports departures from prior optimal-scaling estimates, including development MLM loss increasing with further training for some small-data settings.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures development-set MLM loss across model sizes, corpus sizes, and training checkpoints, and reports estimates for low-resource compute and data choices. It also evaluates downstream NLU performance. The cited results from Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are not recorded as this study's results. MLM loss values are shown in figures but are not given numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: Trains 36 BERT MLM models (16M/51M/124M params × 5M/25M/125M words × 4 languages) for ~hundreds to thousands of epochs. It measures dev MLM loss across checkpoints and FLOPs, plus downstream NLU. It compares its empirical optima with values computed from Kaplan and Hoffmann and argues those allocations do not hold in low-resource, multi-epoch settings. This is an argued departure from the originals' allocations, so T5; it is also a new setting (encoder-only, repeated data).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that optimal model/data/compute estimates from Kaplan and Hoffmann do not hold in low-resource settings, and that data needs are higher: tokens should exceed parameters, roughly an order of magnitude above Hoffmann. Hoffmann's model-size estimates are close to theirs. At fixed compute, larger, under-trained models are preferred, in line with Kaplan. They recommend using all available text and pretraining for hundreds of epochs. Larger models overfit small corpora in pretraining loss, but this does not propagate to downstream tasks. Results are consistent across languages and tasks except QNLI.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains encoder-only BERT models with masked language modeling in low-resource settings, rather than reproducing the original autoregressive-language-model scaling experiments. It compares three model sizes and three corpus sizes across four languages.
record.method_sensitivity: Language, pretraining corpus size, model size, and training duration affect the results. The authors also note that the low-resource corpus sources differ across languages.
record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2023
record.problems: Only three model sizes and three corpus sizes are tested; the low-resource setting is simulated; corpus composition differs between language groups; and common BERT-base hyperparameters are used for smaller models without tuning. MLM loss values are presented in plots rather than numerically.
record.rows_left_out: The separately reported downstream scores in Tables 3–7 and 11–13 are not itemized row by row; the study's stated aggregate trends and QNLI exception are recorded instead. The MLM loss trajectories at 125M words are not itemized by model and language. Tables 14–17 are included as discrete optimum estimates, but no power-law fits are reported.

untested.parts: Power-law form, exponents, and range over several orders of magnitude; only 3 sizes per axis.
Whether the optimal N and D grow as a stable power of compute; no fit is made.
Entire version; shape is scaled jointly, and the paper assumes Kaplan's shape result.
Other modalities, fine-tuning/transfer scaling, and moderate repetition.
A fitted mapping from scale or loss to downstream score.

missing.what: Numeric dev MLM losses at 100K vs 500K steps for BERT16M and BERT51M at 5M, with matched downstream scores showing loss–downstream decoupling
MLM accuracy grid: BERT51M beats BERT124M at 25M in all languages; BERT16M at 125M is no better than at 25M (eu/es/sw)
Fixed-compute comparison (~1e19 FLOPs): BERT124M at 200K steps beats BERT51M at 500K steps on 11/16 tasks, supporting Kaplan's larger-model preference

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'reversed' state on V1 for the rising-loss rows was wrong, because V1 excludes data-bottlenecked runs; these rows are relinked to V5 (repetition) and V7. The Kaplan/Hoffmann comparison values in Tables 14–17 are computed by the authors (exponents a=0.73 and a=0.5). Several Kaplan values (e.g., 257 tokens) look misapplied. The study's 'optimal' values are bounded by its 3×3 grid. Words and tokens are conflated.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fit or report power-law exponents for loss against parameters, tokens, or compute, and does not establish the law over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
The study reports discrete low-resource recommendations and a comparison at comparable compute, but does not fit stable powers of compute for optimal parameter and token counts.
Model depth, width, and other architecture details are scaled together rather than varied at fixed parameter count.
No non-text modality or fine-tuning/transfer scaling-law test is conducted.
The study reports downstream task trends across its tested languages, models, and data sizes, but does not fit a predictive mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.
The study compares low-resource results with earlier estimates and reports non-monotonic loss curves, but does not vary parameter-counting conventions or fitting methods.
